blocks.text: Quick verdict

Webshare is cheaper at small, steady volumes: $27.50 for 10 GB against $35, and it supports SOCKS5 and 24-hour sticky sessions with a published pool size. Rayobyte is cheaper at scale and for irregular usage: about $200 for 100 GB against $225, $0.90/GB from a terabyte, and traffic that never expires while Webshare's allowance resets every 30 days. Rayobyte also sells mobile proxies, which Webshare does not. Pick on your volume pattern.

Webshare and Rayobyte are both popular with cost-conscious scraping teams, and both sell strong datacenter catalogs alongside residential proxies. Webshare offers cheap monthly residential allowances, SOCKS5, a free datacenter plan and an 80M+ advertised pool. Rayobyte offers residential traffic that never expires and steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB, but its residential gateway is HTTP(S) only. This comparison works through which model is cheaper for steady and for irregular usage.

blocks.text: Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is built for developers who want to configure everything themselves. Pricing is transparent, the free datacenter plan makes it easy to test integrations, and paid plans scale smoothly from tiny to large. Its residential network advertises 80M+ IPs across 195 countries. It does not sell mobile proxies or a broad scraping API, and paid plans start with an account-wide limit of 500 concurrent requests.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: Webshare vs Rayobyte

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

At 10 GB a month, Webshare is the cheaper option at about $27.50 against $35 for Rayobyte, roughly 21% less. For a 100 GB month, Rayobyte costs about $200 while Webshare costs about $225, so Rayobyte saves around 11%. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while Webshare's allowance does not (allowance resets every 30 days; no rollover). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Webshare lists '80M+' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Webshare lists 195 countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Webshare supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Webshare's favour. On sessions, Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Webshare: low prices and a developer-friendly API. With Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. Run the same small test on both before committing.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Webshare: fine for light rank tracking. Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: Webshare wins. The deciding factor for Webshare: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. The limitation on the Webshare side: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: fewer carrier or ASN controls. The limitation on the Webshare side: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.
Tight budgets: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. How Rayobyte compares: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Webshare and Rayobyte before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Webshare vs Rayobyte faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Webshare comes out ahead in 2, Rayobyte in 2, and 2 are ties. With no overall winner, decide on the factor that matters most to you: Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
